title: Power
summary: Main breaker trips, brownouts, Kraken current limits, loose PDH and breaker terminals, battery.

options.label: Main breaker tripped in a match
Robot is dead, no lights anywhere
One device or channel has no power
Radio or RIO reboots when the robot drives
PDH status light is not green

drive-motors.question: Does the drivetrain use Kraken X60 or Falcon (Talon FX) motors?

kraken-limits.title: Main breaker trip: Kraken supply current limits
steps: Most main breaker trips this season were Kraken or Falcon drive motors left on the default 70 A supply current limit. Eight swerve motors at 70 A is far past the 120 A main breaker.
Set SupplyCurrentLimit on the drive motors to 50 to 60 A with SupplyCurrentLimitEnable true. Steer motors 20 to 30 A. Confirm in Phoenix Tuner X after deploy.
A stator limit alone does not protect the breaker. The supply limit is the one that matters here.
Try to rotate each crimped lug on the breaker. Tighten any that turns. A hot loose lug trips early.
Redeploy and run the drivetrain against a wall for a few seconds. Watch total current in the DS log or PDH.

steps.text: Does the main breaker still trip?
steps.yes: Swap the breaker and check the battery leads.

main-breaker-other.title: Main breaker trip: other causes
steps: Try to rotate each lug on the main breaker by hand. Tighten any that turns. Loose lugs heat the breaker and trip it below rating.
Check the battery connector and leads. Wiggle them. Tie-wrap the connector halves together.
Ask what the robot was doing when it tripped. A stalled arm, pinned drivetrain, or mechanism against a hard stop draws full stall current.
Set supply current limits on every drive and mechanism motor. Spark MAX 40 to 60 A on drive. Talon FX 50 to 60 A.
Breakers age. One that has tripped many times trips easier. Swap it for a new 120 A breaker.

steps.yes: Read per-channel current in the DS log viewer with the team.

battery-voltage.question: What does the DS show for battery voltage with the robot disabled and resting?

weak-battery.title: Weak battery
steps: Swap to a fully charged battery. A good battery rests at 12.5 V or more.
Retire the battery if it has been dropped or is more than 2 seasons old.
Check the battery leads and connector. A loose crimp reads low under load even on a full battery.
Use a battery beak or load tester if the team has one. Under 12.0 V loaded means retire it.

steps.text: Does the voltage still read low?
steps.yes: Charge every battery before each match.

brownout-wiring.title: Brownout with a good battery
steps: Open the DS log. Find the voltage dip. Under 6.8 V the RIO cuts outputs. Under 6.3 V (RIO 1) or 6.75 V (RIO 2) everything disables.
Wiggle the battery connector and main breaker lugs. Try to rotate each lug. Loose main power is the top cause after motors.
Squeeze the wires at the PDH or PDP main terminals. Confirm the bolts are tight with split washers.
Lower motor supply current limits. Drive first, then any mechanism that starts from stall.
Put the RIO on its own channel. A shared channel with a motor pulls it down.

steps.text: Does the robot still brown out with motors idle?
steps.yes: Swap the battery and check the main power path.

dead.question: Is the main breaker pushed in and the battery connector fully mated?

dead-fixed.title: Breaker or battery was not connected
steps: Push the main breaker in until it clicks. Mate the battery connector until it seats.
Tie-wrap the battery connector halves together so it cannot pull apart in a match.

steps.yes: Push the breaker fully off and back on.

dead-robot.title: Robot dead with breaker in and battery connected
steps: Check the battery at the terminals with a meter. Under 10 V is a dead battery. Swap it.
Measure from the battery through the breaker to the PDH or PDP. No voltage after the breaker means a dead breaker or a broken lug crimp.
Look at the PDH or PDP status LED. Dark with 12 V on the main terminals means the board is dead or reverse polarity.
Check for a wire pulled out of the main terminal or a broken battery lead crimp.
Swap the breaker for a known good one.

steps.text: Is the PDH still dark with 12 V on the main terminals?

channel.title: One channel has no power
steps: On the PDH, a red channel LED means no voltage and a fault. Check the breaker is pushed fully in or the fuse is seated.
A blinking red channel LED is a sticky fault from an earlier trip. Push the breaker in and clear faults.
Tug the Weidmuller wires on that channel. Pull, strip, and reseat.
Swap the breaker or fuse for a known good one of the same rating.

steps.text: Does the channel still have no power?
steps.yes: Check the switchable channel is not off waiting for code.

reboot-under-load.title: Radio or RIO reboots under load
steps: Squeeze and wiggle the wires at the PDH or PDP main terminals and the main breaker. A loose terminal drops voltage under load.
Tug the RIO and radio power plugs. Reseat with fresh stripped copper. Tie-wrap the cables.
Remove one power source if the radio has both PoE and DC power.
Check the DS log for the voltage dip. Under 6.3 V the RIO can reset. Lower motor supply current limits.
Put the RIO and radio on their own channels, not shared with a motor or compressor.

steps.text: Does it still reboot under load?
steps.yes: Swap the battery and the breaker.

pdh-lights.title: PDH status light
steps: Blue solid: powered, no CAN comms. Check the CAN wires and that robot code is running.
Orange and yellow blinking: CAN fault. Check the bus and the PDH termination jumper.
Orange and blue blinking: low battery. Swap the battery.
Orange and magenta blinking: over current on the board. Find the stalled device.
Magenta blinking: keep alive timeout. Code stopped talking to it. Restart robot code.

steps.text: Is the light orange and cyan (a hardware fault)?
